steps.title: Scatter diagrams and \(r\)
steps.body:
Pearson’s \(r\) describes a linear relationship between two variables:
•  sign: positive if \(y\) tends to rise with \(x\), negative if it falls
•  size: \(|r|\) close to \(1\) means the points lie close to a straight line; close to \(0\) means little linear relationship
•  range: \(-1\le r\le1\), with no units; changing the units of \(x\) or \(y\) does not change \(r\)

Rough words for the exam: \(|r|>0.8\) strong, \(0.5\) to \(0.8\) moderate, below \(0.5\) weak. Always give both the strength and the direction: “strong positive”.

steps.title: What \(a\) and \(b\) mean in context
steps.body:
Exam questions ask you to “interpret” the parameters. Say what they mean for these variables, with units:
•  \(a=4.69\): for each extra hour of revision, the score increases by about \(4.7\) marks (on average)
•  \(b=37.6\): the predicted score for a student who revises for \(0\) hours is about \(38\) marks

Two cautions:
•  \(b\) can be meaningless if \(x=0\) is outside the data, e.g. a “height at age 0”
•  the words are “associated with” or “on average”, not “causes”

steps.title: Using the line to predict
steps.body:
Substitute the \(x\)-value into the equation. Then say how much to trust the answer:
•  interpolation: \(x\) inside the range of the data, and \(|r|\) strong, so the prediction is reliable
•  extrapolation: \(x\) outside the range of the data, so the prediction is unreliable, however strong \(r\) is; the pattern may not continue

The line of \(y\) on \(x\) is for predicting \(y\) from \(x\). Using it backwards, to predict \(x\) from a given \(y\), is not appropriate.

steps.title: The mean point, and correlation is not causation
steps.body:
Two facts that appear in exam questions:
•  the regression line of \(y\) on \(x\) always passes through the mean point \((\bar x,\,\bar y)\). Given \(\bar x\) and the equation, you can find \(\bar y\) without the data, and vice versa.
•  a strong correlation does not show that \(x\) causes \(y\). A third factor may drive both, or the direction may be the other way round.

Also: \(r\) measures linear relationships only. A clear curve can have \(r\) near \(0\); always look at the scatter diagram.

questions.stem:
Eight students recorded the number of hours, \(x\), they slept before a test and their score, \(y\), in the test.
\(\begin{array}{c|cccccccc} x & 4 & 5 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 7 & 8 & 9 \\ \hline y & 52 & 58 & 60 & 65 & 70 & 72 & 78 & 84 \end{array}\)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient, \(r\), and describe the correlation.
parts.figCap: The points rise together and lie close to a line: strong positive.
wrongs: That is the gradient of the regression line.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the equation of the regression line of \(y\) on \(x\).
wrongs: \(27\) is \(b\), the intercept; the first box asks for the gradient.
\(0.157\) is the gradient of \(x\) on \(y\): the lists are the wrong way round.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Use the regression line to estimate the score of a student who slept for \(6.5\) hours.
parts.figCap: Up from 6.5 to the line, across to 68.2: interpolation.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: A student slept for \(12\) hours. Comment on the reliability of using the regression line to estimate this student’s score.
opts: Not reliable: \(12\) is outside the range of the data (extrapolation), and the line would give \(103\), an impossible score
Reliable: \(r\) is very close to \(1\)
Reliable: the line passes through \((\bar x,\,\bar y)\)
parts.bad: A strong \(r\) does not justify extrapolation: \(12\) hours is well outside \(4\) to \(9\), and the line gives \(103\), which cannot be a score out of \(100\).
parts.figCap: The data runs from x = 4 to 9; x = 12 is far to the right of it.
ms: not reliable, since \(12\) is outside the range of the data (extrapolation)

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: Interpret the meaning of the gradient of the regression line in this context.
opts: Each extra hour of sleep is associated with an increase of about \(6.33\) marks in the score
A student who sleeps \(6.33\) hours scores full marks
The score is \(6.33\) times the hours slept
parts.bad: The gradient is the change in \(y\) for each unit increase in \(x\): about \(6.33\) more marks for each extra hour of sleep.
parts.figCap: The slope: rise of 6.33 marks per hour.
ms: for each additional hour of sleep…

questions.stem:
A café owner records the daily temperature, \(x\) °C, and the number of iced drinks sold, \(y\), on seven days.
\(\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} x & 10 & 12 & 15 & 18 & 20 & 24 & 27 \\ \hline y & 30 & 36 & 44 & 50 & 57 & 66 & 74 \end{array}\)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the equation of the regression line of \(y\) on \(x\).
wrongs: That is \(b\); the first box asks for \(a\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Estimate the number of iced drinks sold on a day when the temperature is \(22\) °C.
parts.figCap: x = 22 lies inside 10 to 27: interpolation, reliable.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: The owner wants to estimate the temperature on a day when \(100\) drinks were sold, using this regression line. Comment on this.
opts: Not appropriate: \(100\) is outside the data range, and the line of \(y\) on \(x\) should not be used to predict \(x\) from \(y\)
Appropriate: rearrange the line to make \(x\) the subject
Appropriate, because \(r\) is so close to \(1\)
parts.bad: Two problems: \(100\) drinks is well beyond the data (\(30\) to \(74\)), and a \(y\)-on-\(x\) line is for predicting \(y\); predicting \(x\) needs the \(x\)-on-\(y\) line.
parts.figCap: y = 100 is far above the highest data value, 74.
ms: extrapolation: \(100\) is outside the range of the data
the \(y\) on \(x\) line is not appropriate for estimating \(x\)

questions.stem: A set of \(10\) data pairs \((x,\,y)\) has \(\bar x=5.2\) and \(\bar y=31\). The regression line of \(y\) on \(x\) has equation \(y=4.1x+b\), and the correlation coefficient is \(r=0.93\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.figCap: No data points given: the line passes through the mean point (5.2, 31).
ms: the line passes through \((\bar x,\,\bar y)\): \(31=4.1\times5.2+b\)
wrongs: That is \(\bar y\); substitute the mean point into the line.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: The \(x\)-values are converted to new units by \(X=10x\). Write down the gradient of the regression line of \(y\) on \(X\), and the value of \(r\) for the new data.
parts.figCap: Stretching the x-axis by 10 divides the gradient by 10; the fit, and r, are unchanged.
ms: \(r\) does not depend on the units of \(x\)
wrongs: \(41\) multiplied: each new unit is one tenth of an old one, so the rise per unit is one tenth. Divide.
\(r\) has no units and does not change.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: An eleventh data pair, far from the regression line, is added to the data. State the effect on \(r\).
opts: \(|r|\) decreases: the points are less close to a straight line
\(r\) is unchanged
\(r\) increases
parts.bad: A point far from the line weakens the linear relationship, so \(|r|\) moves towards \(0\).
parts.figCap: One point well off the line pulls r towards 0.

apply.lostMarksHint: most lost marks here are the direction word missing from “strong positive”, predicting outside the data, and interpreting the gradient without the context.
